#24518. Breaking: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1922 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass owners’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass owners’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Manufacturer insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” remarked Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

It has been revealed that the revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational manufacturer with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any firm operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly people until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting owners to open the app and place orders, they stated.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it noted it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” noted Hyppönen.

Recent findings suggest that the app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers mentioned.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

Recent findings suggest that in China, about three quarters of smartphone owners are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

It has been revealed that “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he mentioned.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

In a recent development, toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

It has been revealed that according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to people’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

In a recent development, of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews demonstrated that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” remarked René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread rapidly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new enhancement of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the revision, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

Sources indicate that the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the manufacturer’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the revision, noted although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

It has been revealed that the Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

Breaking: Campaigners back call for scrutiny of consent laws by Joanne Young

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Experts say no law states third-party consent is a valid defence and call for public debate and further education.
  • Campaigners have welcomed a call for scrutiny of consent laws by a survivor of drug-facilitated rape but remarked action must also focus on wider issues around sexual assault.
  • Joanne Young, who was drugged and raped by her husband and sexually abused by men he invited into their home, warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Experts say no law states third-party consent is a valid defence and call for public debate and further education.

Campaigners have welcomed a call for scrutiny of consent laws by a survivor of drug-facilitated rape but remarked action must also focus on wider issues around sexual assault.

Joanne Young, who was drugged and raped by her husband and sexually abused by men he invited into their home, warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.

Philip Young, 50, advertised Joanne Young, his then wife, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

As four men were convicted of sexual offences against her on Thursday, Young, 49, remarked: “No one should be able to give [consent] on your behalf.” Her daughter, Alex Young, also called for a change in the law to make it clear that third-party consent cannot ever be used as an argument in a court of law.

Barristers and campaigners said there was no law that stated third-party consent was a valid defence as they called for a public debate and further education about consent.

Kate Parker, a criminal barrister and founder of the charity Schools Consent Project, said: “The law currently has nothing in it which allows someone to point to another person and say: ‘Because of what they told me, I believed the other person to be consenting.’ You can’t effectively outsource consent to a third party, the law has never had that within it. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 certainly doesn’t have that in it.

“What is instead happening is defence counsel in this case, and in cases like this, are pointing to a defence you can run, which is to say that the defendant genuinely and reasonably thought that the victim was consenting.”.

Sources indicate that the trial heard that the four men, who were strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her. The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

Parker mentioned it was right that a defendant should be able to say what was in his or her mind at the time of an alleged offence.

“I think that’s a sort of cornerstone of our law. But I hope that these arguments carry less and less traction with juries when generally there is more knowledge as to what the laws around consent are,” she remarked.

“I hope that as time goes by, juries become more aware and members of the public become more aware as to what the law on consent is, so no one can say: ‘Because a third party told me so and I acted on it, I thought I was legally safe.’”.

Harriet Wistrich, a solicitor and the director of the Centre for Women’s Justice, mentioned the jury in the Young case had ultimately rejected the defence.

It has been revealed that “It should be obvious in the law that somebody can’t consent on somebody else’s behalf. But you could explicitly make it the case,” she said.

“Defence barristers should robustly defend their clients. That’s their job. But they shouldn’t overstep the mark by relying on myths and stereotypes.”.

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, agreed the law on consent should be scrutinised. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states: “A person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice.”.

Industry observers note that she said: “We can look at strengthening existing laws. But really we have to get to the root of the problem, which is about the understanding of consent.

It has been revealed that “The existing law is already clear. This is about how that law is interpreted and it is regularly misinterpreted and misapplied. That happens all the time by defendants, by barristers, by juries, and so this is highlighting a lack of understanding that consent is specific: it’s not a one-time event, it’s ongoing, it’s highly dependent on the actual situation at the time. The fact that someone is unconscious necessarily means they can’t consent.

“The other thing about these cases is that drugging someone is the opposite of consent. What is emerging from these organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse cases is a growing recognition of the attraction that some people have to a woman not being able to consent.”.

Prof Miranda Horvath, the director of the Institute for Social Justice and Crime at the University of Suffolk, noted incorrect beliefs about consent should be “robustly challenged”.

“It is incredibly vital that people understand that legally nobody can give consent on your behalf, and this underlines the importance of clear education on consent through society, from young people right through to adults,” she mentioned.

“Rape and serious sexual offences are a direct choice made by perpetrators, and a lack of understanding on whether a sexual partner has given consent cannot be an acceptable excuse.”.

In a recent development, the Labour MP Jess Phillips said the government should look at whether the law should be tightened. “It is absolutely right that the government should strength-test whether there is a way of really asserting in the law that consent cannot ever come from a third party – we need to be absolutely satisfied that that is the case,” she said.

In a recent development, “There is an argument that while the law states that consent cannot come from a third party, we still see it being used as a defence. Perhaps if we look at tightening the law, these men would have had to plead guilty and Joanne Young would have been spared this trial.”.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson mentioned: “The law is clear: no one can consent on someone else’s behalf. Consent must come from the person themselves, and they must have the freedom and capacity to make that choice. We keep the criminal law under review, and we will always look at what more can be done to protect victims.”.

#24515. Breaking: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3719 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US.
  • The rules prevent the import or sale of all latest router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US.
  • In a recent development, while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all latest router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

In a recent development, while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese manufacturer and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link indicates.

Sources indicate that TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

Industry observers note that TP-Link has pledged to assemble all newly introduced routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

According to recent reports, some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

In a recent development, the Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any upcoming technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie mentioned in a joint statement.

The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

The US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”.

Recent findings suggest that for the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, fresh additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List presently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

“The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”.

McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

“The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”.

Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre remarked the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

Sources indicate that mcIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any company receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she said.

TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft noted in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

It has been revealed that security expert Bruce Schneier mentioned there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier said.

In a recent development, with routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”.

It has been revealed that when asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese manufacturer, Schneier remarked that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”.

In a recent development, TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier noted that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”.

TP-Link indicates the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article said, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”.

According to recent reports, TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the company doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

It has been revealed that TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, remarked in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

According to recent reports, “TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he stated. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese manufacturer. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”.

TP-Link remarked in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”.

Industry observers note that in 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

TP-Link’s response to Joyce said it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The organization indicates in a fact sheet that when routers provided to users by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”.

In a recent development, florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”.

Sources indicate that last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

“Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

Sources indicate that TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the manufacturer’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

“Any time a tech giant has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” remarked Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

Recent findings suggest that marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a company has larger issues pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he said.

Sources indicate that although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a organization official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he said.

“There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he said. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”.

According to recent reports, kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the organization’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

It has been revealed that kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”.

Sources indicate that kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the organization’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he said. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”.

In a recent development, kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he said. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”.

Sources indicate that kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”.

Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a blueprint to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency aims if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”.

Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not currently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”.

Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she noted others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring aims.

“I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she said.

The FCC mentioned the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”.

Although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

Recent findings suggest that after the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre stated.

Under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

“We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC said in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”.

According to recent reports, the FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

“The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill says.

In a recent development, the CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement said the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”.

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Industry observers note that walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

Sources indicate that "The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

Industry observers note that "This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey stated Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Industry observers note that walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the tech giant performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

According to recent reports, walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also mentioned Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said.

It has been revealed that sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It stated its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

Industry observers note that furner told CNBC the upcoming membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The organization on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company noted it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey mentioned Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

It has been revealed that the big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

In a recent development, gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also remarked Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

Dickson mentioned the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson stated this upcoming approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Industry observers note that net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the manufacturer said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson stated in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson stated.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

Industry observers note that at Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the tech giant attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

The tech giant's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson noted it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.

According to recent reports, the Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its latest CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

In a recent development, banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the tech giant attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson said the brand has since introduced fresh products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

In a recent development, "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he remarked. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.
  • Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
  • The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, stated a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

Recent findings suggest that one Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he stated. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”.

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

In a recent development, genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa stated during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, noted the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

In a recent development, the case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that indicated attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

Sources indicate that in January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Industry observers note that refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later demonstrated had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric challenges of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” stated Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”.

Recent findings suggest that legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention indicates the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have remarked gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

Industry observers note that the court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.

Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

According to recent reports, the former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

It has been revealed that during a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.

Sources indicate that “This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”.

According to recent reports, israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already mentioned Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Sources indicate that washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

The US state department stated in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.

It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and noted it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

Industry observers note that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the tech giant's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The tech giant intends to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz remarked on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

It has been revealed that paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The company has stated it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world.
  • There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
  • In a recent development, for almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world.

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

In a recent development, for almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

It has been revealed that by the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a major thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Sources indicate that salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, remarked: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”.

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, mentioned they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

Sources indicate that “Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”.

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

Sources indicate that they immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” remarked Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She noted, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”.

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

Recent findings suggest that “We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

Yellowjackets is back. With Season 4 comes newly introduced mysteries and new opening title cards inviting viewers to speculate on what's next. With each episode, Mashable will be probing these details, looking for questions and their answers. So, buckle up.

The theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more. Some images are classic, like pre-crash footage of the team smiling and Jackie (Ella Purnell) smirking on the soccer pitch and drawing a threatening finger across her neck. But others are new.

In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:.

In a recent development, melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

Under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

It has been revealed that at the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

Sources indicate that the colors of this shot are brighter and more saturated than Yellowjackets tends to go. The uniform is a throwback 1950s style, and actress Tawny Cypress is smiling in a wide-eyed way that's not in keeping with Taissa's character. So, we're speculating this will be another dream sequence or vision. This one feel Lynchian, and as his work touches on doomed romances and the dark underbelly of suburbia, one can assume he'd speak to Taissa on both levels. But what does it mean?

Her face is covered by a mask, but there's no mistaking her frizzy blond hair and glasses. Will the girls' return to civilization show Misty's path to working at the old folks home? Or will this be a dream sequence where she imagines what her future might be?

In a recent development, in the credits, it's a close-up of what appears to be Shauna, wearing a blindfold and holding a string. To get a fuller context, you have to look to the sneak peek images Paramount released on Nov. 5.

There you can see a wider shot:.

Recent findings suggest that here you can see she's holding a knife on a string while standing inside the crashed plane, her team huddled on the floor around her. This recalls the ritual seance the girls did in Season 1 in the cabin's attic. They'd tried to contact the presumed dead owner of the cabin, and instead tapped into something darker and more mysterious.

The swinging knife is meant to answer the girls' questions. So, are they calling on the "it" of the wilderness for advice ahead of their rescue?

In a recent development, whose head is being pried open in this nightmarish way? It's hard to tell from the close-up, which gives away no facial features. Dark hair and a sleeve ending in lace are the only clues. But based on the outrageousness, we're going to guess this one is a nightmare within the show.

This set dressing was spotted by fans on Reddit eight months back. But what's its role in the show? Well, we know Jackie's parents have money. Could this be how they memorialize their golden girl?

That's probably bad news for Shauna, right?

Christina Ricci's been a violent ax-wielder before. (We remember Lizzie Borden Took an Ax and The Lizzie Borden Chronicles). We also know an ax is how Edwin died last season — though by Lottie's hand. Yet despite Misty's maniacal facial expression, and her still wearing Natalie's leather jacket, we're guess this is more a Misty-to-the-rescue moment. Maybe she's about to pull a Shining and ax a door?

In a recent development, where is she? WHO IS SHE AIMING AT?

It has been revealed that as this is shot comes from the opening scene of Season 4, there's not much mystery here. Teen Jeff (Jack DePew) had moved on from Shauna and Jackie, getting high with Randy (Riley Baron) and working at Jackie's parents' furniture story. Then he sees her face on the news, with reports of their rescue.

With Shauna finally coming back from the wilderness, we're likely to see how grief and love brought these two together for a marriage we may not envy, but kind of admire?

#24501. Latest Update: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes
